blocks.text: Second, distinguishing the substance, in two. First, the statement of the heading.

inline.s: [Commentary] Second, distinguishing the substance.

[Sub-commentary] 'Second, distinguishing the substance' is that which in the earlier general list was said: 'The Vaipulya real-form is the substance.' The Vaipulya real-form has two senses. First, this sutra was spoken in the third, the Vaipulya period, when the four teachings of the Vaipulya are all discussed together, and this sutra belongs to the Round; it distinguishes that this sutra's real-form is not the real-form of the Avatamsaka, Prajna, or Lotus periods—hence it is called Vaipulya. Again, the real-form of the Round teaching: every gate can enter the pool of coolness; hence 'fang' (the expanded). Living beings and Buddhas both possess it, equal and non-dual; hence 'deng' (the equal). The commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says, 'The substance is the essential substance.' The Miaozong Chao says, 'The name is on the side, a guest; the substance is the main, the host. The name is a provisional name; the substance is the real substance. Every name has beneath it its substance. Now we distinguish the real substance beneath the provisional name.'

blocks.text: Second, the explanation, in two. First, citing the treatise to make clear the substance.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Treatise of Great Wisdom says: 'All Mahayana sutras universally take the single real-form as their proper substance.'

[Sub-commentary] The Miaozong Chao says: 'All dharmas are unproduced and unextinguished, neither existent nor non-existent, neither a doer nor an object; they leave the characteristics of words, leave the characteristics of names, leave the characteristics of the mind's conditions. Leaving these characteristics is called the real-form, the form of the formless.' If we bring back that meaning to this sutra, then the first section from 'seven rows of railings' down to 'those who hear this sound all give rise to the thought of the Buddha, the thought of the Dharma, and the thought of the Sangha' makes clear the Pure Land that is the mind—what the preface calls 'the bejeweled groves and jade-like pools directly reveal the mind-source.' The middle section from 'For what reason is that Buddha named Amitabha' down to 'It can only be spoken of as immeasurable, unbounded asamkhyeyas' makes clear the Amitabha of the self-nature—what the preface calls 'the measure of longevity and the light fully manifest the self-nature.' 'The bejeweled groves and jade-like pools' reveals the dependent retribution, which includes the four kinds of Pure Land; 'the measure of longevity and the light' and so on reveals the proper retribution, which includes the Buddhas and bodhisattvas and the people of the nine grades of rebirth. This is precisely the Lotus teaching's 'only the Buddha and the Buddhas can exhaust the real-form of all dharmas'; it is what Tiantai calls 'the nature endowed with the three thousand, none of which is outside the substance of the real-form.'

blocks.text: Second, concluding what is expressed.

inline.s: [Commentary] This is the principle expressed.

blocks.text: Third, making clear the cardinal purport, in two. First, the statement of the heading.

inline.s: [Commentary] Third, making clear the cardinal purport.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation, in two. First, citing the scripture to establish it.

inline.s: [Commentary] The scripture says: 'If there be one who believes, he should make the vow to be reborn in that land.'

[Sub-commentary] In the earlier general list it was said that faith, vows, and pure karma are the cardinal purport. Hence now the scripture is cited to establish it. 'If there be one who believes' is the gate of faith. 'He should make the vow' is the gate of vows. To establish the practice-gate of pure karma, one should also cite the following passage, 'Holding the name for seven days, single-minded and unconfused, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.' These are the gates of the three essentials. Faith is the faith that there is a Pure Land that is the mind, an Amitabha that is the self-nature, and the Tathagata's vow-power, through which all may attain rebirth. This corresponds to the first of the ten vehicles, 'contemplating the inconceivable realm.' Though there be this faith, if there is no vow, one cannot be reborn. For since Amitabha by his vow-power already gathers living beings, I should make the vow to seek rebirth, so that there is the natural relation of the essential nature and the effortless giving and taking away, like a magnet naturally attracting. Judged among the ten vehicles, this is the second, 'truly giving rise to the bodhi-mind.' Among the four universal vows, when it is 'the Buddha way is supreme, and I vow to accomplish it,' this includes the three preceding vows. Though there be this vow, if there is no practice-gate, the vow becomes wild. Hence one must hold the name for seven days, single-minded and unconfused. Gathering this within the ten vehicles, it is the third, 'skillfully settling the mind in calming and insight.' Holding the name for seven days is insight; single-minded and unconfused is calming. Just at the moment of holding the name is the single mind; just at the moment of the single mind is the holding of the name. Thus calming and insight both illumine and both suspend; in skillfully settling the mind, one achieves it. This briefly marks out the three methods for those of superior faculties; the remaining seven vehicles are all included within them.

blocks.text: Second, concluding as the cardinal purport.

inline.s: [Commentary] This is the cardinal purport of the whole sutra.

blocks.text: Fourth, making clear the function, in two. First, the reminder.

inline.s: [Commentary] Fourth, discussing the function.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation, in two. First, citing the scripture to establish it.

inline.s: [Commentary] The scripture says: 'They immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Bliss, and all are non-retrogressing from supreme bodhi.'

[Sub-commentary] The first two lines show the passage after 'Holding the name for seven days, single-minded and unconfused.' The next two lines are the earlier scripture's 'Those reborn there are all avivartika.' The earlier general list said that the forsaking of suffering and the obtaining of joy is the function, which is the scripture's text 'they immediately attain rebirth' and so on. If we use the later to complete the earlier, then 'those reborn there' are all the Saha beings who practice Buddha-recitation, and they must attain non-retrogressing bodhi. These two passages together establish the function and power of this sutra.

blocks.text: Second, concluding as the function and power.

inline.s: [Commentary] To depart from the suffering of birth-and-death and obtain the joy of liberation: this is the function and power of this sutra.

[Sub-commentary] The other gateways all cause living beings to exit the three realms vertically, departing the suffering of birth-and-death and obtaining the joy of liberation—like a nine-story tower from which one ascends higher and higher; when the strength is sufficient one advances, and when the feet tire one falls, so the ascent is difficult. Only the Pure Land gateway causes living beings to exit the three realms horizontally, departing the suffering of birth-and-death and obtaining the joy of liberation—like a home's threshold, from east to west; a glance and it is seen, a snap of the fingers and one is there, so the going is easy. Is not the function and power of this sutra great?

blocks.text: Fifth, judging the doctrinal classification, in two. First, the general statement.
Fifth, judging the doctrinal classification.

inline.s: [Sub-commentary] 'Teaching' is the sage's words addressed to those below; 'classification' is the distinguishing of same and different. The Tathagata established the teaching in the five periods, advancing according to the time; the great and the small, the gradual and the sudden, each have their divisions. Tiantai distinguishes them according to the five periods, and each has its rationale. Hence whenever one explains a sutra, one must judge its doctrinal classification.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the classification.

inline.s: [Commentary] The division belongs to the Mahayana Vaipulya teaching; according to the meaning of the two storehouses, it is included in the bodhisattva-storehouse; dividing gradual and sudden, it belongs to the sudden teaching.

[Sub-commentary] In judging this doctrinal classification there are three statements. 'The division belongs to the Mahayana Vaipulya teaching' is the first, judging by the period. The earlier general list said that the Mahayana raw ghee is the doctrinal classification; raw ghee is the Vaipulya period. The Tiantai Great Master used the Nirvana five periods, in their arising order, to judge the whole teaching of the Tathagata's single transformation. First, from the cow comes milk—an analogy for the Buddha's very first, in the twenty-one days, preaching the Avatamsaka Sutra. Next, from milk comes curds—an analogy for the twelve divisions bringing forth the nine divisions of sutras, and for the twelve years in which he preached the four Agamas of the lesser vehicle. Next, from curds comes raw ghee—an analogy for the Agamas bringing forth the Vaipulya; in eight years he preached the Vimalakirti, the Great Collection, the Surangama, the Lankavatara, the sixteen Contemplations, and this sutra, refuting the one-sided and censuring the lesser, extolling the greater and extolling the Round. The shravakas obtain the benefit of the refutation and rebuke, ashamed of the lesser and aspiring to the greater, entering and departing without difficulty. For example, the lesser vehicle's one-sided emptiness, outside the three realms, has no body and no land; now he specially tells Shariputra that Amitabha has a land, the bodhisattvas have a body, and those reborn there are all non-retrogressing—this is precisely that matter. Next, from raw ghee comes ripened ghee—an analogy for the Vaipulya bringing forth the Prajna; in twenty-two years he preached the great Prajna and other sutras, using the water of the emptiness-wisdom to wash away the two-vehicle practitioners' attachments, causing Subhuti and others to turn and teach the Prajna, bestowing the wealth and melting it together. Next, from ripened ghee comes the finest cream—an analogy for the Prajna bringing forth the Lotus and the Nirvana; the nine realms and the three vehicles are united in the provisional and given the prophecy, with none small and none great, all caused to become Buddhas. Now this is the third, raw ghee; hence it is said that the division belongs to the Mahayana Vaipulya teaching. 'According to the meaning of the two storehouses, it is included in the bodhisattva-storehouse' is the second, judging by the storehouse. The sutras spoken by the Buddha include the shravaka-storehouse—those spoken for the two-vehicle practitioners—whose principle reaches only the true truth, whose delusion only breaks views and thoughts, whose wisdom only cultivates the emptiness-contemplation, and whose fruit has no body and no land. Since this sutra makes clear that apart from the Saha there is a separate Pure Land, then its fruit-reward has a body and a land; is it not that its principle, delusion, wisdom, and fruit all belong to the bodhisattva-storehouse? 'Dividing gradual and sudden, it belongs to the sudden teaching' is the third, judging by the teaching. The teachings of the transformation-manner are gradual and sudden. The gradual requires eons of cultivation to reach non-retrogression; the sudden accomplishes it in this very life, reaching the station of avivartika. Hence it concludes: 'to cause ordinary beings not to retreat from bodhi.' Yet to cause them in this very life to reach the station of non-retrogression is indeed a Round and Sudden teaching; but one must first open the Round understanding, then cultivate the Round practice, break the three delusions, and then realize the Round fruit, in order to reach non-retrogression. Now it merely speaks of the proper and dependent retribution of that land, to serve as the opening of understanding and the generating of faith; and the holding of the name for seven days, single-minded and unconfused, to serve as the gateway of practice; and at the end of life, immediately attaining rebirth, to reach non-retrogression. Unless it were Shakyamuni's skillful means, Amitabha's vow-power, the practitioner's past roots, the three essentials at present, and single-mindedness unconfused in fully subduing and at once cutting off the three delusions and the root of karma, and advancing straight ahead without turning—how could one accomplish this? Hence know that this sutra is the supreme cream for the evil world of the five turbidities. The Nirvana Sutra says: 'Poison placed in raw ghee; eating it at once kills.' How could one not believe it?

blocks.text: Second, the translator, in two. First, the statement of the section.
Second, the translator's title.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumarajiva of the Yao Qin, by imperial command
Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two. First, making clear his birthplace.

inline.s: [Commentary] Kumarajiva, here meaning 'Child-lifespan,' was a man of the kingdom of Kucha.

blocks.text: Second, making clear his translation.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Later Qin's Yao family held Chang'an, honored him as the national teacher, and in the Hongshi period he translated the various sutras and treatises.

[Sub-commentary] 'Yao Qin' distinguishes it from the fallen Qin, the Former Qin, and the Qifu Qin; this is the Later Qin of the Yao family. It was in the third year of Hongshi that he entered Chang'an. The Qin lord commanded the monk Xian and others, eight hundred shramanas, to receive Kumarajiva's instruction. At the Caotang Temple he translated sutras and treatises, in all ninety-eight works, comprising four hundred twenty-one scrolls; Sengrui, Sengzhao, Daochang, and others took down the translation.

blocks.text: Third, attesting to his merit.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Nanshan Gan Tong Zhuan says: 'The sutra-translating master since the seven Buddhas.'

[Sub-commentary] The past seven Buddhas all were born in western India, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. After their nirvana, whether in the period of the right Dharma or of the semblance Dharma, the Sanskrit texts of the West were sure to be transmitted to China, and translated from Sanskrit into Chinese. Translating masters have existed in every age; only Master Kumarajiva, from the time of the seven Buddhas, has always been the sutra-translating master for our China. This was said by the Nanshan Vinaya Master on the question put by Master Fei, the celestial being. Some also say that Master Kumarajiva's station attested to the three worthies. Hence we know he was no ordinary man.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the scripture-text, in two. First, the total and separate sectioning; second, the explanation according to the sections. Now the first has two. First, the total sectioning into three divisions.

Second, the scripture-text in three divisions. From the beginning to 'the great assembly were all gathered' is the preface division. From 'At that time the Buddha told' to after the six directions, where the scripture-title is adduced and explained, is the main-teaching division. From 'You should all believe and accept my words' to the end of the text is the circulation division.

inline.s: [Sub-commentary] Since the Han Ming Emperor, when the sutras came to China, those who spread the teaching expounded them following the text, without any sectioning. It was the Jin Master Dao'an who first divided the greater and lesser sutras, all having three divisions—the preface, the main teaching, and the circulation. Later, when the western sastra on the Bodhisattva's Illumination arrived, its three divisions accord with this. Again, the renunciates of this land since the Han all followed their teacher's surname, as with the three Zhi. Later Master Dao'an said that since one has left one's lay surname to follow Shakyamuni, all should be joined under the single surname 'Shi.' Later, when the Ekottara Agama arrived, the World-honored One indeed said: 'A thousand streams entering the sea all have one salty flavor; the four castes that leave home are all called Shakyamuni's descendants.' Hence later people praised Master Dao'an: 'His division of the sutras well accords with the sastra of light; his conferring the surname Shi is much like the Ekottara.'

blocks.text: Second, the separate statement of the two prefatory divisions.

inline.s: [Commentary] All sutras have both the common and the separate prefatory divisions. This sutra has only the common preface—the attestation of faith—and no separate preface of initiation; it is, among the twelve divisions, the 'taught without being asked.'

[Sub-commentary] The two prefatory divisions: 'common' means the same—the six matters such as 'Thus have I heard' are the same in all sutras; hence 'common.' 'Separate' means the different—the initiating circumstances of each sutra are different. Hence this sutra has only the common preface and no separate preface, being the Tathagata's spontaneous teaching without a question. For the Pure Land teaching, if it were aimed at the bodhisattva capacity, it would be precisely what they face and must be spoken upon a question—as in the sixteen Contemplation Sutra, which is such a case. But this sutra is addressed to the supreme vehicle and to the capacities of ordinary beings, to make them know that a subtle body and land are to be obtained in this very life. This was originally not the realm of the lesser vehicle or of ordinary beings; how could they ask of it? Hence the Tathagata, without being asked, spoke it spontaneously, proclaiming in accord with his nature—what need of an initiating circumstance?

blocks.text: Second, the explanation according to the sections, in two. First, the explanation of the common preface, in two. First, the division into sections.
The common preface is in two. First, the five sentences of attestation.

inline.s: [Sub-commentary] 'Attestation of faith': as the Buddha was about to pass into nirvana, Ananda asked, 'At the head of all sutras, what words should be placed?' The Buddha replied, 'Place the words “Thus have I heard” and so on.' Not only I do this—the Buddhas of the three times all open their sutras in this way.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the scripture, in two. First, setting forth the scripture.

inline.s: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anathapindada, in the kingdom of Shravasti.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the meaning, in five. First, the explanation of the dharma-substance indicated.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Thus' points to the dharma-substance heard. The principle of the real-form, the same in ancient and modern times, is called the principle of thusness, and is spoken as 'is.'

[Sub-commentary] 'Thus' is a word pointing to the dharma. What it points to is the dharma-substance heard—the principle of the real-form. Such a principle, the same in ancient and modern times, is called 'thus,' that is, the unmoving substance of suchness, traversing the ten thousand ages yet ever new, passing through a thousand differences yet unchanging. The Tathagata can weigh this principle and speak, without ever being contrary to it; hence it is called 'thus.'

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the one who hears, that is manifested.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'I' is Ananda, who at the compiling of the dharma-treasury said of himself, 'This dharma-gate, I heard from the Buddha.'

[Sub-commentary] The Buddhabhumi Sastra says: at the time of compiling, they jointly requested, saying, 'As you have heard it, so should you speak.' The dharma-transmitting bodhisattva then consented, saying, 'Thus shall I speak, as I have heard.'

blocks.text: Third, the explanation of the capacity and response that are made clear.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'At one time' is the time when the capacity and the response unite. The reason a specific year, month, or day is not stated is that the two lands' calendars differ.

[Sub-commentary] The capacity is Ananda and the twelve hundred, together with the bodhisattvas and the rest; the response is Shakyamuni Tathagata, the able teaching-lord. Without the response the capacity cannot be accomplished, and without the capacity the response cannot be fulfilled; only when the anvil and the mallet strike together is the vessel formed. When the capacity and the response are united, then this sutra is spoken. 'The two lands' calendars differ'—as with the four seasons of this land versus the three times of the other, or East China reckoning the first of the month by the dark of the moon, while the West reckons it by the full moon. Since the two regions are thus, one can infer for the four border peoples; it is hard to fix, so it says only 'at one time.'

blocks.text: Fourth, the explanation of the teaching-lord named.

inline.s: [Commentary] 'Buddha' means awakening. Self-awakening differs from the non-awakening of ordinary beings; awakening others differs from the solitary awakening of the two vehicles; the completion of awakening differs from the bodhisattvas in their causal stage. Honored among the many sages, he is therefore called the Buddha—that is, Shakyamuni the teaching-lord.

[Sub-commentary] The Sanskrit 'Buddha' here means 'the Awakened One'—one who has awakened to the nature and the characteristics, the true and the false—that is, the ultimate original awakening and the ultimate initial awakening. 'Self-awakening differs from the non-awakening of ordinary beings': ordinary beings are dazed and disturbed all day, following falsehood and drifting; the Tathagata is serene and illumined in merged union, reverting to the source and returning to the root. 'Awakening others differs from the solitary awakening of the two vehicles': the two vehicles, having awakened to birth-and-death, leap alone like a stag; the Tathagata himself reaches the other shore and, in his compassionate ferry, ferries beings across. 'The completion of awakening differs from the bodhisattvas in their causal stage': the bodhisattvas, though cultivating the three awakenings, have not completed the three causes; the Tathagata has completely fulfilled the three awakenings and perfectly manifested the three virtues. Being honored among the two-vehicle practitioners and the bodhisattvas, among the many sages, he is called the Buddha. Following the particular from the generic, he is the Saha teaching-lord, Shakyamuni Buddha.

blocks.text: Fifth, the explanation of the abode described, in two. First, the explanation of the kingdom of Shravasti.

inline.s: [Commentary] Shravasti, properly Sravasti, here means 'the land of renown,' spoken of because its people and things were wealth-abundant and famous far among the kingdoms.
[Sub-commentary] 'Its people and things were wealth-abundant' means this kingdom was complete in the things of the sense-desires and wealth, and abundant in those who heard much and were liberated.

blocks.text: Second, the explanation of the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anathapindada, in two. First, setting forth the names and virtues of the two persons, in two. First, Jeta.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Sanskrit 'Jeta' here means 'victory'; it is the name of the prince of King Prasenajit.
[Sub-commentary] When the prince of King Prasenajit was born, it chanced that they had just won a victory over a foreign kingdom; hence this fine name was given.

blocks.text: Second, Sudatta.

inline.s: [Commentary] The Sanskrit 'Sudatta' here means 'good giving'; it is the name of an elder, who could bestow gifts on the poor of the land and was named 'the giver to the orphaned and solitary.'

blocks.text: Second, making clear the joint naming of the two persons.

inline.s: [Commentary] He spread gold sideways to buy the garden from Jeta, established a monastery, and invited the Buddha to teach; Jeta donated the trees; hence the two are named together.

[Sub-commentary] The elder Sudatta, arranging a marriage for his son, went to Rajagrha and there saw the Tathagata; he invited the Buddha to accept offerings. The Buddha told Shariputra to go with him to look at a site. Only Prince Jeta's park, with its flourishing trees, could be made into a monastery. Jeta jestingly consented: if he covered the ground with gold bricks laid sideways, and hung the forest with gold coins, then he would give it. Sudatta, delighted, had carts carry gold to spread over the ground, nearly filling it. Jeta, seeing his sincerity, said, 'The ground should belong to you; the trees belong to me. Let us together offer them to the Buddha—would that not be good?' Hence afterwards, whenever a sutra was spoken at this place, the compilers of the sutra, setting forth the location, always praise the virtue of the two and name them together.
